# Section A — The trapezium rule

## Question 1 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.78em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">[4 marks]</span>

::: {.question}
Let $f(x)=\ln x$ on the interval $[1,4]$, with $n=3$ equal intervals.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Write down the trapezium estimate in exact form, and the exact value of
$\displaystyle\int_1^4\ln x\,\mathrm dx$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** State which way the error goes, and justify it **without** comparing the two numbers.
:::

**(a)** With $h=1$ and ordinates at $x=1,2,3,4$:

$$T=\tfrac12\bigl(\ln1+2\ln2+2\ln3+\ln4\bigr)=\tfrac12\bigl(4\ln2+2\ln3\bigr)=2\ln2+\ln3=\ln12 . \tag*{[1]}$$

*The $\ln 4$ at the right-hand end is $2\ln 2$, which is what makes the whole estimate collapse to a single
logarithm.* Numerically $\ln 12\approx2.4849$.

$$\int_1^4\ln x\,\mathrm dx=\Bigl[x\ln x-x\Bigr]_1^4=(4\ln4-4)-(0-1)=8\ln2-3\approx2.5452 . \tag*{[1]}$$

**(b)** $f'(x)=\dfrac1x$ and $f''(x)=-\dfrac1{x^{2}}<0$ for every $x$ in $[1,4]$. **[1]**

*So $\ln x$ is concave down on the whole interval, every chord lies below the curve, and the trapezium rule
therefore gives an **underestimate** — no comparison of the two numbers is needed.* **[1]**

(Consistently, $\ln 12<8\ln2-3$.)

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-cap: "Q1. y = ln x is concave down on [1,4], so each of the three chords lies below the curve and the estimate falls short."
xs = np.linspace(1, 4, 400)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 3.3))
ax.plot(xs, np.log(xs), color=BLUE, lw=2, label=r"$y=\ln x$")
nd = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
ax.plot(nd, np.log(nd), color=RED, lw=1.6, marker="o", ms=5, label="trapezium chords")
for n in nd:
    ax.plot([n, n], [0, np.log(n)], color=RED, lw=0.8, alpha=0.5)
ax.fill_between(nd, np.log(nd), 0, color=RED, alpha=0.12)
ax.fill_between(xs, np.log(xs), np.interp(xs, nd, np.log(nd)), color=BLUE, alpha=0.18)
ax.set_xlabel("x"); ax.set_ylabel("y")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper left")
ax.grid(alpha=0.18)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## Question 2 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.78em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">[4 marks]</span>

::: {.question}
Consider these statements about a function $f$ on $[a,b]$:

&nbsp;&nbsp;$P$: the trapezium rule with $n$ equal intervals produces an **overestimate** of
$\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm dx$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;$Q$: $f''(x)>0$ for $a\le x\le b$.

Is $P$ necessary for $Q$, sufficient for $Q$, both, or neither? Justify **both** directions, giving an
explicit counterexample where one fails.
:::

**$Q\Rightarrow P$.** If $f''>0$ throughout $[a,b]$ the curve is concave up, so every chord lies **above** the
graph and every strip is overestimated. *A sum of overestimates is an overestimate,* so $Q$ implies $P$ and
**$P$ is necessary for $Q$**. **[2]**

**$P\not\Rightarrow Q$.** Take $f(x)=x^{4}-x^{2}$ on $[-1,1]$ with $n=1$. The chord joins $(-1,0)$ to
$(1,0)$, so $T=0$, while

$$\int_{-1}^{1}\bigl(x^{4}-x^{2}\bigr)\,\mathrm dx=2\left(\tfrac15-\tfrac13\right)=-\tfrac4{15}<0 ,$$

so the rule **overestimates** and $P$ holds. But $f''(x)=12x^{2}-2$ gives $f''(0)=-2<0$, so $Q$ fails. **[2]**

**$P$ is necessary but not sufficient for $Q$.** *This is the mirror image of the exam question — the same
asymmetry, with the inequality the other way up.*

## Question 3 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.78em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">[3 marks]</span>

::: {.question}
Find a function $f$ on $[0,2]$ which is **not** a straight line but for which the trapezium rule with $n=2$
gives the **exact** value of $\displaystyle\int_0^2 f(x)\,\mathrm dx$. Explain in one sentence why it works.
:::

Take $f(x)=(x-1)^{3}$. **[1]**

$$T=\tfrac12\bigl(f(0)+2f(1)+f(2)\bigr)=\tfrac12(-1+0+1)=0,
\qquad
\int_0^2 (x-1)^{3}\,\mathrm dx=\left[\tfrac{(x-1)^{4}}{4}\right]_0^2=0 . \tag*{[1]}$$

*The curve has rotational symmetry about $(1,0)$, the midpoint of the interval: it is concave down on $[0,1]$
and concave up on $[1,2]$, so the shortfall on the left strip is exactly the excess on the right and the two
errors cancel.* **[1]**

This is the "inflection inside" row of the memorise box — the rule is exact by cancellation, not because the
function is linear.

# Section B — "Necessarily true" with a discriminant

## Question 4 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.78em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">[4 marks]</span>

::: {.question}
Let $n(k)$ be the number of distinct real solutions of

$$x^{2}+2kx+3k-2=0 .$$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Build the complete map of $n(k)$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Which of these are **necessarily true**?

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** $n(k)=0$ for $k=1$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **II** $n(k)=2$ for $k<0$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**III** $n(k)=0$ for $\tfrac54<k<\tfrac74$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **IV** $n(k)=2$ for $k>2$
:::

**(a)** $\Delta=(2k)^{2}-4(3k-2)=4k^{2}-12k+8=4\bigl(k^{2}-3k+2\bigr)=4(k-1)(k-2)$. **[1]**

| | condition on $k$ | $n(k)$ |
|---|---|---|
| $\Delta>0$ | $k<1$ or $k>2$ | **2** |
| $\Delta=0$ | $k=1$ or $k=2$ | **1** |
| $\Delta<0$ | $1<k<2$ | **0** |

**[1]**

**(b)**

| | claim | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **I** | $n(k)=0$ for $k=1$ | **false** — $\Delta=0$ there, so $n=1$ |
| **II** | $n(k)=2$ for $k<0$ | **true** — $(-\infty,0)$ lies inside $k<1$ |
| **III** | $n(k)=0$ for $\tfrac54<k<\tfrac74$ | **true** — that interval lies inside $(1,2)$ |
| **IV** | $n(k)=2$ for $k>2$ | **true** |

**[2]**

*II, III and IV are each true because the stated range is **contained in** a region of the map, not because it
fills one. I is the usual slip: $\Delta=0$ gives a repeated root, which is still one real solution.*

## Question 5 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.78em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">[4 marks]</span>

::: {.question}
Let $n(k)$ be the number of distinct real solutions of

$$kx^{2}-4x+k=0 .$$

Build the complete map of $n(k)$. **One value of $k$ needs separate treatment — say which, and why.**
:::

**The value needing separate treatment is $k=0$**, because then the $x^{2}$ term vanishes and the equation is
not a quadratic at all. **[1]**

- **$k=0$:** the equation is $-4x=0$, which is linear with the single solution $x=0$, so $n(0)=1$. **[1]**
- **$k\ne0$:** $\Delta=16-4k^{2}=4\bigl(4-k^{2}\bigr)$, so **[1]**

| | condition on $k$ | $n(k)$ |
|---|---|---|
| $\Delta>0$ | $-2<k<2$, $k\ne0$ | **2** |
| $\Delta=0$ | $k=-2$ or $k=2$ | **1** |
| $\Delta<0$ | $k<-2$ or $k>2$ | **0** |

**[1]**

*Collecting, $n(k)=1$ at the three values $k=-2,\,0,\,2$ — and the middle one is there for a completely
different reason from the other two.* Writing $\Delta=16-4k^{2}$ and stopping would wrongly give $n(0)=2$.

# Section C — Logarithms

## Question 6 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.78em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">[5 marks]</span>

::: {.question}
A student solves $\log_2(7x-3)=1+2\log_2(x-1)$ as follows.

| | |
|---|---|
| Step 1 | $\log_2(7x-3)-2\log_2(x-1)=1$ |
| Step 2 | $\log_2(7x-3)-\log_2\bigl((x-1)^{2}\bigr)=1$ |
| Step 3 | $\dfrac{7x-3}{(x-1)^{2}}=2$ |
| Step 4 | $2x^{2}-11x+5=0$ |
| Step 5 | $(2x-1)(x-5)=0$ |
| Step 6 | $x=\tfrac12$ or $x=5$ |

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** State the domain of the original equation.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Identify the **first** step at which the solution set changes, and prove it by showing a
value that satisfies that step but not the one before it.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Give the correct solution.
:::

**(a)** Both logarithms must exist: $7x-3>0$ and $x-1>0$, so the domain is $\boxed{x>1}$. **[1]**

**(b)** The first change is at **Step 2**. *It replaces $2\log_2(x-1)$, which requires $x>1$, by
$\log_2\bigl((x-1)^{2}\bigr)$, which requires only $x\ne1$ — a strictly larger domain, so the two equations
cannot have the same solution set.* **[2]**

Proof by exhibiting $x=\tfrac12$:

- **Step 2:** $7x-3=\tfrac12>0$ and $(x-1)^{2}=\tfrac14>0$, and
  $\log_2\tfrac12-\log_2\tfrac14=-1-(-2)=1$ ✓
- **Step 1:** requires $\log_2(x-1)=\log_2\bigl(-\tfrac12\bigr)$, which does not exist ✗

**[1]**

**(c)** From Step 3, $7x-3=2(x-1)^{2}=2x^{2}-4x+2$, so $2x^{2}-11x+5=0$ and $(2x-1)(x-5)=0$, giving
$x=\tfrac12$ or $x=5$. Only $x=5$ lies in the domain, so $\boxed{x=5}$. **[1]**

## Question 7 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.78em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">[3 marks]</span>

::: {.question}
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** For which real $x$ is $\log_b\bigl(x^{3}\bigr)=3\log_b x$ true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** For which real $x$ is $\log_b\bigl(x^{4}\bigr)=4\log_b x$ true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Explain in one sentence why the two answers differ, and state the version of the identity
for $x^{4}$ that is valid for every $x\ne0$.
:::

**(a)** $\log_b\bigl(x^{3}\bigr)$ needs $x^{3}>0$, which for real $x$ means $x>0$; $3\log_b x$ needs $x>0$.
The two domains **agree**, so the identity is true for $\boxed{x>0}$ — and both sides are undefined
elsewhere. **[1]**

**(b)** $\log_b\bigl(x^{4}\bigr)$ needs only $x\ne0$, while $4\log_b x$ still needs $x>0$. So the identity
holds for $\boxed{x>0}$, but the left-hand side is defined on a **larger** set. **[1]**

**(c)** *An odd power preserves the sign, so $x^{3}>0$ says the same thing as $x>0$; an even power destroys
the sign, so $x^{4}>0$ is satisfied by negative $x$ too, and that is the extra territory where the right-hand
side has nothing to say.* The version valid for every $x\ne0$ is

$$\log_b\bigl(x^{4}\bigr)=4\log_b\lvert x\rvert . \tag*{[1]}$$

## Question 8 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.78em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">[4 marks]</span>

::: {.question}
Solve $\log_4(x+3)+\log_4(x-3)=1$, stating the domain first and justifying any root you reject.

Then find the complete set of values of $a$ for which

$$\log_5(x+a)=1+\log_5(x-2)$$

has exactly one real solution.
:::

**First equation.** Domain: $x+3>0$ **and** $x-3>0$, so $x>3$. **[1]**

$$\log_4\bigl((x+3)(x-3)\bigr)=1\ \Rightarrow\ x^{2}-9=4\ \Rightarrow\ x^{2}=13\ \Rightarrow\ x=\pm\sqrt{13}.$$

*The root $x=-\sqrt{13}$ makes both original logarithms undefined — it appears only because the product
$(x+3)(x-3)$ is positive there as well.* So $\boxed{x=\sqrt{13}}$. **[1]**

**Second equation.** Domain: $x>2$ (and then $x+a=5(x-2)>0$ automatically). **[1]**

$$x+a=5(x-2)\ \Rightarrow\ 4x=a+10\ \Rightarrow\ x=\frac{a+10}{4}.$$

*The equation is linear once the logarithms are removed, so there is at most one candidate; it is a genuine
solution exactly when it lies in the domain:*

$$\frac{a+10}{4}>2\ \Longleftrightarrow\ a>-2 .$$

So there is exactly one solution precisely when $\boxed{a>-2}$, and none when $a\le-2$. **[1]**

# Section D — The ambiguous SSA case

## Question 9 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.78em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">[5 marks]</span>

::: {.question}
A triangle $ABC$ has $AB=10$, $BC=2\sqrt{10}$ and $\angle BAC=\theta$, where $\cos\theta=\tfrac45$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Show that two non-congruent triangles are possible.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Find both possible values of $AC$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Find the ratio of the area of the larger triangle to the area of the smaller, **without**
computing either area.
:::

**(a)** From $\cos\theta=\tfrac45$ with $\theta$ acute, $\sin\theta=\tfrac35$. The distance from $B$ to the
ray $AC$ is

$$h=AB\sin\theta=10\cdot\tfrac35=6 .$$

Since $BC=2\sqrt{10}\approx6.325$ and $AB=10$,

$$6<2\sqrt{10}<10,$$

so $h<BC<AB$ and there are exactly two non-congruent triangles. **[2]**

**(b)** Cosine rule on $\angle A$, with $AC=x$:

$$40=10^{2}+x^{2}-2(10)(x)\tfrac45
\ \Rightarrow\ x^{2}-16x+60=0
\ \Rightarrow\ (x-6)(x-10)=0,$$

so $AC=6$ or $AC=10$. **[2]**

**(c)** *Both triangles share $AB$ and the angle at $A$, so the perpendicular height from $B$ to the line
$AC$ is the same in each; taking $AC$ as the base, the areas are therefore in the ratio of the bases.*

$$10:6=\boxed{5:3} \tag*{[1]}$$

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-cap: "Q9. The two triangles share AB and the angle at A, so B sits at the same height above the base line; only AC differs, 10 against 6."
th = np.arccos(4/5)
A = np.array([0.0, 0.0]); B = 10*np.array([np.cos(th), np.sin(th)])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.2))
for xc, col, lab in [(10, GREEN, "C₂ (AC = 10)"), (6, RED, "C₁ (AC = 6)")]:
    C = np.array([xc, 0.0])
    ax.fill([A[0], B[0], C[0]], [A[1], B[1], C[1]], color=col, alpha=0.16)
    ax.plot([B[0], C[0]], [B[1], C[1]], color=col, lw=2)
    ax.plot(*C, "o", color=col, ms=6)
    ax.text(C[0]-0.3, -0.9, lab, color=col, fontsize=9)
ax.plot([A[0], 11.5], [0, 0], color=GREY, lw=1.0)
ax.plot([A[0], B[0]], [A[1], B[1]], color=BLUE, lw=2.2)
ax.plot([B[0], B[0]], [0, B[1]], color=GREY, lw=1.0, ls=":")
ax.text(B[0]+0.25, B[1]/2, "h = 6", color=GREY, fontsize=8.5, rotation=90, va="center")
ax.plot(*A, "o", color="black", ms=5); ax.text(-0.6, -0.2, "A", fontsize=11)
ax.plot(*B, "o", color="black", ms=5); ax.text(B[0]-0.1, B[1]+0.4, "B", fontsize=11)
ax.set_xlim(-1.5, 12); ax.set_ylim(-1.8, 8)
ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## Question 10 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.78em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">[3 marks]</span>

::: {.question}
A triangle $ABC$ has $AB=8$ and $\angle BAC=60^{\circ}$. Find the complete set of values of $BC$ for which
there are exactly **two** non-congruent such triangles. Give the endpoints exactly, and say what happens at
each endpoint.
:::

$$h=AB\sin\theta=8\sin60^{\circ}=8\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt3}2=4\sqrt3 . \tag*{[1]}$$

Two non-congruent triangles exist exactly when $h<BC<AB$:

$$\boxed{4\sqrt3<BC<8} \tag*{[1]}$$

**At the endpoints.** *At $BC=4\sqrt3$ the circle of radius $BC$ about $B$ is tangent to the ray, so the two
solutions merge into one right-angled triangle. At $BC=8$ the circle passes through $A$ itself, so one of the
two intersections is the degenerate point $C=A$ and only one genuine triangle survives.* **[1]**

## Question 11 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.78em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">[3 marks]</span>

::: {.question}
A triangle $ABC$ has $AB=5$, $BC=4$ and $\angle BAC=\theta$ with $\sin\theta=\tfrac45$. How many
non-congruent triangles are there? Name the special feature of the one (or ones) that exist.
:::

$$h=AB\sin\theta=5\cdot\tfrac45=4 . \tag*{[1]}$$

Here $BC=4=h$ exactly, which is the boundary row of the table, so there is **exactly one** triangle. **[1]**

*The circle of radius $4$ about $B$ touches the ray rather than cutting it, and the point of contact is the
foot of the perpendicular from $B$ — so the triangle is right-angled at $C$.* **[1]**

# Section E — Necessary and sufficient among a family

## Question 12 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.78em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">[5 marks]</span>

::: {.question}
Let $x$ be a real number, and consider

$$A:\ \lvert x\rvert<3,\qquad B:\ 0<x<2,\qquad C:\ x^{2}<4,\qquad D:\ x<5,\qquad E:\ \lvert x+1\rvert<1 .$$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Write each as an interval and draw all five on one number line.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Which statement is a **necessary** condition for exactly three of the other four?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Which statement is necessary for **all** four?
:::

**(a)**

| | statement | interval |
|---|---|---|
| $A$ | $\lvert x\rvert<3$ | $(-3,3)$ |
| $B$ | $0<x<2$ | $(0,2)$ |
| $C$ | $x^{2}<4$ | $(-2,2)$ |
| $D$ | $x<5$ | $(-\infty,5)$ |
| $E$ | $\lvert x+1\rvert<1$ | $(-2,0)$ |

**[2]**

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-cap: "Q12. D swallows everything; A swallows B, C and E but not D, because D runs past 3."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 3.0))
rows = [("A:  |x| < 3", -3, 3, BLUE),
        ("B:  0 < x < 2", 0, 2, GREEN),
        ("C:  x² < 4", -2, 2, AMBER),
        ("D:  x < 5", -6.6, 5, RED),
        ("E:  |x+1| < 1", -2, 0, "#6b46c1")]
for i, (lab, lo, hi, col) in enumerate(rows):
    y = len(rows) - i
    ax.hlines(y, lo, hi, color=col, lw=5, alpha=0.75)
    ends = [hi] if lo < -6.5 else [lo, hi]
    ax.plot(ends, [y]*len(ends), "o", color=col, ms=5, mfc="white")
    if lo < -6.5:
        ax.annotate("", xy=(-7.1, y), xytext=(-6.6, y), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=col))
    ax.text(-7.6, y, lab, fontsize=9, ha="right", va="center", color=col)
ax.axvline(0, color=GREY, lw=0.7)
ax.set_xlim(-11.5, 6.0); ax.set_ylim(0.3, 5.7)
ax.set_yticks([]); ax.set_xticks([-3, -2, 0, 2, 3, 5]); ax.set_xlabel("x")
ax.grid(axis="x", alpha=0.2)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**(b)** Count what each one **contains**:

| statement | contains | count |
|---|---|---|
| $A=(-3,3)$ | $B$, $C$, $E$ | **3** |
| $B=(0,2)$ | — | 0 |
| $C=(-2,2)$ | $B$, $E$ | 2 |
| $D=(-\infty,5)$ | $A$, $B$, $C$, $E$ | 4 |
| $E=(-2,0)$ | — | 0 |

So $\boxed{A}$ is necessary for exactly three of the others. *It misses only $D$, which reaches up to $5$ and
so contains values such as $x=4$ that break $\lvert x\rvert<3$.* **[2]**

**(c)** $\boxed{D}$ is necessary for all four, since every other interval lies entirely to the left of $5$.
**[1]**

## Question 13 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.78em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">[3 marks]</span>

::: {.question}
For the same five statements, **two** of them are each a **sufficient** condition for exactly three of the
other four. Which two? Explain why counting for "sufficient" runs the opposite way to counting for
"necessary".
:::

Sufficient means **smaller**, so now count what each statement is contained **in**:

| statement | is contained in | count |
|---|---|---|
| $A$ | $D$ | 1 |
| $B=(0,2)$ | $A$, $C$, $D$ | **3** |
| $C$ | $A$, $D$ | 2 |
| $D$ | — | 0 |
| $E=(-2,0)$ | $A$, $C$, $D$ | **3** |

So $\boxed{B\ \text{and}\ E}$. **[2]**

*The two counts run opposite ways because "$X$ is necessary for $Y$" and "$X$ is sufficient for $Y$" are the
same implication read from the two ends: $Y\subseteq X$ against $X\subseteq Y$. The widest statement, $D$, is
necessary for everything and sufficient for nothing; the narrowest ones are sufficient for many and necessary
for none.* **[1]**

# Section F — Negating quantifiers

## Question 14 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.78em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">[6 marks]</span>

::: {.question}
Negate each statement. Give the symbolic form **and** the English, and say whether the **original** is true
or false.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** $\forall n\in\mathbb N,\ \exists p\ \text{prime}:\ p>n$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** $\exists x\in\mathbb R,\ \forall \varepsilon>0:\ \lvert x\rvert<\varepsilon$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** $\forall x\in\mathbb R,\ \exists y\in\mathbb R,\ \forall z\in\mathbb R:\ x+y+z>z$.
:::

**(a)** Negation: $\exists n\in\mathbb N,\ \forall p\ \text{prime}:\ p\le n$ — *there is a natural number
that no prime exceeds, i.e. there is a largest prime.* The original is **true** (there are infinitely many
primes), so the negation is false. **[2]**

**(b)** Negation: $\forall x\in\mathbb R,\ \exists\varepsilon>0:\ \lvert x\rvert\ge\varepsilon$ — *every real
number is at least as big as some positive number.* The original is **true**: take $x=0$, since
$\lvert0\rvert=0<\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$. **[2]**

**(c)** Negation: $\exists x\in\mathbb R,\ \forall y\in\mathbb R,\ \exists z\in\mathbb R:\ x+y+z\le z$.
*Since $x+y+z>z$ is just $x+y>0$, the statement does not involve $z$ at all and the inner quantifier is
vacuous.* The original is **true**: given $x$, take $y=1-x$, so $x+y=1>0$. **[2]**

## Question 15 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.78em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">[4 marks]</span>

::: {.question}
Negate, taking care with the implication:

$$\forall n\in\mathbb N,\ \exists m\in\mathbb N,\ \forall k\in\mathbb N:\ \bigl(k>m\ \Rightarrow\ a_k<\tfrac1n\bigr).$$

State in one sentence what the original statement says about the sequence $(a_n)$, and what the negation says.
:::

Flip all three quantifiers and negate the final condition, remembering
$\neg(P\Rightarrow Q)\equiv P\wedge\neg Q$: **[1]**

$$\exists n\in\mathbb N,\ \forall m\in\mathbb N,\ \exists k\in\mathbb N:\quad
k>m\ \ \textbf{and}\ \ a_k\ge\tfrac1n . \tag*{[2]}$$

**What they say.** The original says that for every $n$ the sequence is eventually below $\tfrac1n$ — in
other words the terms are driven below every positive bound, which for a sequence of non-negative terms is
exactly $a_k\to0$. *The negation says there is one fixed $n$ for which $a_k\ge\tfrac1n$ happens infinitely
often, so the sequence keeps coming back up.* **[1]**

*Writing the negation as another implication is the standard error: "$k>m\Rightarrow a_k\ge\tfrac1n$" would be
a different and much weaker statement.*

## Question 16 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.78em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">[3 marks]</span>

::: {.question}
Consider these two statements about a function $f$:

&nbsp;&nbsp;$S_1$: $\forall x\in\mathbb R,\ \exists y\in\mathbb R:\ f(y)=x$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;$S_2$: $\exists y\in\mathbb R,\ \forall x\in\mathbb R:\ f(y)=x$.

Explain in one sentence what each says, give a function for which $S_1$ is true, and explain why $S_2$ is
false for **every** function $f$.
:::

$S_1$ says **every real number is a value of $f$** — $f$ is onto $\mathbb R$. For example $f(x)=x$, or
$f(x)=x^{3}$. **[1]**

$S_2$ says there is a **single** input $y$ whose output $f(y)$ equals **every** real number $x$. **[1]**

*But $f(y)$ is one particular real number, and no number equals both $0$ and $1$. So $S_2$ is false for every
function $f$, whatever $f$ is.* **[1]**

The two statements differ only in the order of the quantifiers, and that order is the whole difference
between "onto" and "impossible".

::: {.callout-tip}
## The six things this sheet was testing

1. The trapezium rule's direction is the sign of $f''$; "underestimate" and "concave down" are **not** the
   same condition, and neither are "overestimate" and "concave up" (Q1–Q3).
2. Build the discriminant map once and test every option against it — and check whether the coefficient of
   $x^{2}$ can vanish (Q4, Q5).
3. The domain is the first line of a log question, and $a\log_b x=\log_b x^{a}$ needs $x>0$ — which bites for
   **even** $a$ only (Q6–Q8).
4. SSA: $h<a<c$ decides the count, the cosine rule on the given angle gives the quadratic, and the area ratio
   is the ratio of its roots (Q9–Q11).
5. Necessary means the larger set, sufficient the smaller — the two counts run opposite ways (Q12, Q13).
6. Flip every quantifier in order, keep the order, and negate the final condition, with
   $\neg(P\Rightarrow Q)\equiv P\wedge\neg Q$ (Q14–Q16).
:::
